extracted.intended_audience: university technology transfer officers, research administrators, IP managers, and counsel handling software and content commercialization
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on copyright doctrines, DMCA provisions, and ISP safe-harbor rules relevant to university-owned or licensed software, databases, and digital works — intended to inform technology transfer, licensing, and commercialization decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-Sale Doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: The first-sale doctrine prevents a copyright owner from interfering with the subsequent use of copies sold; the Copyright Act distinguishes between the copyright and the physical copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Software is generally licensed for use and not sold and, therefore, is not subject to the first-sale doctrine. If the only authorized chain of distribution is by license, purchase from a licensee does not constitute a first sale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Domain
rubrics_metrics.description: When the owner’s right to exclude others from using intellectual property is extinguished for any reason, that intellectual property is said to pass into the public domain and it can be used by anyone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copyright protection does not extend to portions of a work which incorporate preexisting works either copyrighted by others or in the public domain. Copyright law will not bar access to factual data in the public domain. Shareware is not necessarily in the public domain. The open source model uses contract and copyright protection to prevent works from entering the public domain while also preventing the full exercise of exclusive rights under copyright laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merger Doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements of a work which 'must necessarily be used as incident to' the idea, process or system which is the subject of the work are not copyrightable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An idea which can be expressed in only one way is said to have merged with the expression so as to be inseparable; copyright will not bar copying that expression. If idea and expression cannot be separated, only identical copying of the expression is barred (Apple v. Microsoft example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenes á Faire
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright protection does not extend to features required by external factors or to achieve compatibility; stereotyped expression and standard or common features are excluded from copyright protection in the absence of a virtually identical copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The doctrine bars protection for expression dictated by external factors (compatibility, standards); the court noted scenes á faire and the merger doctrine are 'barely distinguishable.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Operation (uncopyrightable functional aspects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional aspects of computer software (as distinguished from expressive aspects) are not eligible for copyright protection; copyright protection does not extend to any 'procedure, process, system, [or] method of operation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Lotus menu command hierarchy held a 'method of operation' (Lotus v. Borland) — copying allowed to preserve interoperability of macros. Aggregation of noncopyrightable elements can itself constitute a method of operation. Enhancements that merely implement company-wide practices by copying rule editors were found uncopyrightable (ILOG v. Bell Logic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright Misuse Defense
rubrics_metrics.description: A copyright holder’s competitive misuse of the copyright can be a defense to copyright infringement and can preclude injunctive relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If licensing terms attempt to suppress competition beyond the scope of copyright (e.g., forbidding development of competing software), courts may find misuse (Lasercomb example). Misuse may preclude preliminary injunctive relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: DMCA Anticircumvention Scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter 12 (DMCA) prohibits circumventing technological measures to control access to a work and creating liability distinct from copyright infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 12 prohibits manufacturing or trafficking in any technology, product, service, or device primarily designed to circumvent (1) a technological measure to control access to a protected work (descrambling/decrypting), or (2) the protection afforded by a technological measure for a right of the copyright owner. DMCA is a statutory framework separate from the definition of copyright infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright Management Information (CMI) rules
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unlawful to provide false copyright management information or intentionally remove or alter any copyright management information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CMI includes title, identifying information about author or copyright owner, terms and conditions for use, or other information the Register may prescribe. CMI does not include personally identifying information about a user. Civil liability applies for violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: DMCA Exemptions — Fair Use and Rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: The anticircumvention prohibition does not automatically allow fair use as a defense; instead, rulemaking by the Librarian of Congress can exempt classes of works for non-infringing uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fair use (17 U.S.C. § 107) applies only to copyright infringement, not to DMCA anticircumvention provisions. The DMCA rulemaking considers impact on criticism, comment, news reporting, teaching, scholarship or research, and effect on market/value of copyrighted works — factors similar to fair use.

rubrics_metrics.name: DMCA Exemptions — Libraries, Interoperability, Research, Security
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific statutory exemptions exist for (i) nonprofit libraries/archives/educational institutions acquiring access solely to determine acquisition, (ii) interoperability reverse engineering to identify program elements necessary for interoperability, (iii) encryption research, and (iv) security testing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Library/university acquisition exemption applies only if a copy is not reasonably available in another form and excludes willful violations for commercial advantage. Reverse engineering exemption limited to identification/analysis of elements necessary for interoperability of independently created programs. Exemptions have limits and conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: DMCA Civil Damages and Remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil remedies for violations of anticircumvention and CMI provisions include injunctive relief, impoundment, damages (actual or statutory), and attorneys' fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory damages for circumvention may range from $200 to $2,500 per act; statutory damages for CMI violations range from $2,500 to $25,000; damages may be trebled if within three years of a prior final judgment for 'another such violation.' Courts may reduce or remit damages if violator had no reason to know acts constituted a violation; remission mandatory for nonprofit libraries fitting the exemption.

rubrics_metrics.name: DMCA Criminal Liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Willful violations of anticircumvention or CMI provisions for commercial advantage or private financial gain can result in criminal penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penalties include fines up to $500,000 or imprisonment up to five years for a first offense, doubled for subsequent offenses; criminal sanctions do not apply to nonprofit libraries, archives, or educational institutions. Criminal proceedings must be commenced within five years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safe Harbor Overview for Internet Service Providers
rubrics_metrics.description: ISPs can be shielded from liability for damages arising from copyright infringement if they register with the Copyright Office and designate an agent to receive notices, and if they meet statutory conditions limiting their role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ISPs lose safe harbor if they: (a) initially placed the material online; (b) generate, select, or alter content; (c) determine recipients; (d) receive a financial benefit directly attributable to a particular act of infringement; (e) sponsor/endorse/advertise the material; or (f) know or are aware via notice or other information indicating the material is infringing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmission Without Modification Safe Harbor Conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: An entity providing transmission, routing, or connections is not liable for intermediate/transient storage or transmission if five statutory conditions are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditions: (1) transmission initiated at direction of third person; (2) automatic technical process without selection by provider; (3) provider does not select recipients except automatically; (4) no copy maintained in manner ordinarily accessible beyond anticipated recipient or for longer than reasonably necessary; (5) material transmitted without modification of its content.

rubrics_metrics.name: System Caching Safe Harbor Conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Intermediate and temporary storage (system caching) of material made available online by a third person is protected if statutory conditions are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditions include: (1) material transmitted without modification; (2) provider complies with rules for refreshing/reloading/updating; (3) provider does not interfere with ability of associated technology to return information that would have been available if obtained directly; (4) provider permits access only to users meeting provider-of-material conditions (e.g., payment/password); (5) provider responds expeditiously to a proper notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: No Benefit and Control (Hosting/Linking) Safe Harbor Conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: A service provider is not liable for information residing at a user's direction or for linking to infringing material if it removes/disabled access expeditiously and lacks certain knowledge/control/financial benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provider must (1) respond expeditiously to remove or disable access and (2) not have (a) actual or implied knowledge of infringement, (b) a financial benefit attributable to the infringing activity, and (c) the right and ability to control the activity. Knowledge is imputed if provider is aware of facts making infringement apparent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice and Takedown — Duty to Remove
rubrics_metrics.description: To qualify for certain safe harbors, an ISP must respond expeditiously to remove or disable access to material claimed to be infringing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if material ultimately is non-infringing, an ISP is not liable for good faith disabling/removal in response to a proper notice or facts making infringement apparent. Substantial compliance with notice provisions is sufficient. Copyright owner is not required to investigate before sending a notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice Required — Elements of a Proper DMCA Takedown Notice
rubrics_metrics.description: A copyright owner’s notice of claimed infringement must contain specified elements to be effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Required: (1) physical/electronic signature on behalf of owner of exclusive right; (2) identification of copyrighted work claimed infringed; (3) identification of claimed infringing material and info reasonably sufficient to permit location; (4) contact info for complaining party; (5) statement of good faith belief that use is not authorized; (6) statement that info is accurate and complainant authorized to act. For caching exception, notice must also confirm removal from originating site or a court order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designated Agent Registration and Public Availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Service providers must designate an agent to receive notices and make that contact information publicly available and registered with the Copyright Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The designated agent’s name, address, phone, and email must be available via the Copyright Office directory and on the service provider’s website in a public location. Designation must be accompanied by a $20 fee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deficient Notice and Provider Responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A deficient notice does not put a service provider on notice of infringing activity unless it identifies the work, claimed infringing material, and contact info and the provider then fails to promptly attempt to contact the complaining party or take reasonable steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notice provider is not liable merely because a notice is insufficient, provided the provider did not knowingly materially misrepresent infringement. Provider must take reasonable steps to attempt contact or otherwise act reasonably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counter-Notification and Replacement Procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: A subscriber whose material was removed may serve a counter notification meeting statutory elements; provider must notify complainant and replace material in a set timeframe unless complainant files an action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counter notice must include: (1) physical/electronic signature of subscriber; (2) identification of removed material and prior location; (3) statement under penalty of perjury that removal was mistake or misidentification; (4) subscriber’s contact info and consent to federal jurisdiction and to accept service of process. Provider must provide copy to complainant and will replace material in ten business days (not less than ten, nor more than fourteen) unless complainant files an action seeking an injunction. Replacement will not subject provider to liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies — Injunctions and Technical Feasibility Considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may order injunctive relief restraining access to infringing material or prohibiting subscriber access, but any order must be the least burdensome effective relief and the court must consider technical feasibility and burden on provider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If provider only provides transmission without modification, court may order blocking access to specific online locations outside the U.S. but may not otherwise restrain provider's system; court must consider technical feasibility and operational burden. Additional limitations apply for institutions of higher education regarding imputation of knowledge from faculty or student activity, subject to statutory conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages for Misrepresentations in Notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person who materially misrepresents that material or activity is infringing or that material was removed by mistake is liable for damages, including costs and attorneys' fees, incurred by injured parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liability applies to alleged infringer, copyright owner, authorized licensee, or service provider injured by reliance on the misrepresentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subpoena Rights and Limits (512(h))
rubrics_metrics.description: A copyright owner can subpoena identifying information for an alleged infringer to protect rights under the Copyright Act, subject to statutory limits and judicial interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subpoena authorizes service provider to provide identifying information available to it. In RIAA v. Verizon, subpoenas cannot be used to obtain user-identifying info if the service provider is merely a conduit under the 512(a) safe harbor and not subject to notice-and-takedown. Subpoenas must identify the material to be removed or disabled.

rubrics_metrics.name: ISP Monitoring, Knowledge, and Secondary Liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Monitoring by an ISP can affect safe-harbor eligibility; knowledge (actual or constructive) can give rise to contributory or vicarious liability for infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualified immunity under DMCA may be denied if monitoring results in a finding that the ISP knew or should have known of infringing material. Courts have found services that profit from infringement or structure business to avoid liability while benefiting financially may be liable (Napster/Aimster/Grokster examples). 'Willful blindness is knowledge.'

rubrics_metrics.name: University Ownership and Scholarly Works Exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Universities often grant faculty ownership of copyright for 'scholarly works,' but certain works (computer software, databases) may not qualify for the scholarly-works exception and ownership should be addressed in a written policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As copyright law evolves and courts narrow protection for software and databases, institutions should have written (and signed) policies specifying ownership to guide commercialization and licensing decisions.
